summary:
Malacca stands under Malaysia's national framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the Federal Penal Code 1936 criminalise same-sex sexual activity with a maximum of twenty years' imprisonment plus whipping, and section 377D, 'outrages on decency', criminalises gross indecency in terms the Human Dignity Trust records as usable against transgender people. These offences are not limited to Malaysian citizens and reach visitors in Malacca.

The Sharia layer reaches Malacca as well. Every one of Malaysia's thirteen states maintains an enactment criminalising cross-dressing or 'a man posing as a woman', with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Those offences apply to Muslims only, are enforced by state Islamic religious departments, and contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing. Three of the thirteen states also bar women from posing as men.

Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. The Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and sixteen Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving the Penal Code offences fully intact; a High Court had already refused to declare the Sharia cross-dressing prohibition unconstitutional. A constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014, following the mass arrest of sixteen trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Enforcement is documented as active rather than dormant. The Human Dignity Trust profile, last updated in 2024, records evidence of the law being enforced in recent years and a crackdown on the LGBT community since the 2018 election. The Human Rights Watch report of 10 August 2022, produced with Justice For Sisters, concludes that pervasive official antipathy toward sexual and gender diversity shapes law enforcement, judicial outcomes and public discourse.

Transgender people in Malaysia are documented as particularly vulnerable to physical and verbal abuse, against a backdrop of consistent reports of discrimination and violence. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months, and case documentation records police mistreatment and impunity. In 2021 the prominent transgender woman Nur Sajat was prosecuted in Selangor and fled the country after threats of arrest, subsequently receiving UNHCR protection; 122 religious officers had been mobilised against her for 'insulting Islam'.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor in Malacca, the Sharia cross-dressing offences do not apply, but the Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B, with media pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details leaked; more than 130 people were held at one point, including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened, and a magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground. Police raided a second sauna in Penang days later.

There is no same-sex marriage, no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination law in Malaysia. Visible gender nonconformity in Malacca is exposed to the same public-morality and religious enforcement that operates nationwide, and the heritage-tourism setting offers no recorded protection.
tangentialFactors:
The official climate described by Human Rights Watch is one of active restriction rather than passive disapproval: government-sponsored 'rehabilitation' and conversion programmes, officials shutting down LGBT events, and censorship of events and media content. Government-funded mukhayyam 'rehabilitation' retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021.

Enforcement carries explicit political backing. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his 'full licence to carry out its enforcement actions' against transgender persons, a directive the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked.

The federal Sharia codes in the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya, cited by Human Rights Watch, typically criminalise same-sex activity and gender nonconformity in the same terms as Malacca's own enactments, so the state-level exposure described here is not unusual within the country.

Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform at national level, and on 2 December 2025 the Home Minister floated revisiting the section 377B provisions, an indication that tightening rather than repeal is under consideration. Human Rights Watch further finds that antipathy toward sexual and gender diversity influences family behaviour and public discourse alongside official decision-making.
localsOnly:
Malaysian citizens and residents who are Muslim fall under their state's Sharia cross-dressing offence in addition to the Penal Code, and are subject to investigation by the state Islamic religious department, which operates with no statutory definition of the conduct it polices.

Resident trans people face documented exposure through the state machinery: the Nur Sajat prosecution of 2021, the July 2020 enforcement licence issued to Jawi, and government-funded mukhayyam retreats constitute the resident-facing enforcement stack that a visitor bypasses only by virtue of not being Muslim and not being a long-term resident.

Residents have no legal route to gender recognition, no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation, and no hate-crime provision covering anti-trans violence; the Klang killing of 25 June 2019 was documented alongside police mistreatment and impunity.

Family and community consequences are part of the resident picture: Human Rights Watch records that pervasive antipathy toward sexual and gender diversity shapes family behaviour and public discourse, not only official action, and that officials shut down community events.
outOfScopeNotes:
Neither the Human Dignity Trust Malaysia profile nor the Human Rights Watch report of 10 August 2022 provides a Malacca-specific breakdown. Arrest, raid and prosecution figures for Malacca itself are not sourced in the current inventory, and the enforcement pattern described here is drawn from national and other-state records.

Whether Malacca's Islamic religious department has issued recent public enforcement directives, comparable to the July 2020 statement by the Religious Affairs Minister regarding Jawi, is unresolved in the available sources.

Section 377D is recorded as drafted in terms that can be used against transgender people, but case-level application of that section to trans defendants in Malacca is not documented here.

Sourching on gender-marker change procedures, healthcare access and venue-level hostility within Malacca is absent from the inventory; the practical position of an visibly gender-nonconforming visitor outside raid situations is therefore inferred from national reporting rather than measured locally.
